# Polishing the transcript

> Use when a video's transcript needs proofreading or polishing - fix typos and mishearings, unify terms and names, fix punctuation and sentence breaks, and write back with word timings unchanged. Do it before translating or captioning. Not for cutting verbal tics (editing) or text unrelated to video.

The transcript the user has was heard by a machine: names misspelled, terms misheard, punctuation scattered, a long stretch of speech strung together with commas. What they want is a base text they can safely build on: captions break lines by it, translations split sentences by it, documents are exported from it. Polishing is a copyedit read straight through from start to finish: correct what was misheard, fix the punctuation, and keep what the speaker said the way they said it.

There are two easy ways to get it wrong. One is changing too much: turning speech into written prose along the way, deleting verbal tics, tightening rambling sentences, even translating the foreign words mixed in. The text looks better, but the captions no longer match the audio, and what viewers hear is not what they read. The other is moving a sentence's text onto other words, or adding or deleting words: every word carries its timing, and once words shift, the timing of the whole stretch of captions is wrong.

## 1. When to do it

- **Before translating and building caption layers.** Sentences are split by punctuation, so changing punctuation changes the sentence splits; once the splits change, the sentence fingerprints recorded by the translation no longer match. So polish and write back first, then `cuccut documents read` again to get the new sentences to translate.
- When this video already has a translation, most sentences will need retranslating after polishing. Tell the user this first, then start.
- Skip it when the user says not to polish, or the transcript has already been polished (the user edited it, or it was done in this session). When polishing is skipped, still do the speaker naming of section 7.

## 2. Change only word for word

Use `cuccut documents read` to read the transcript of kind speech (when there are several, match the one the user means by its source asset). The body's words are a sequence of words, each with an id, start and end times, a speaker and text; punctuation is attached to the words' text: sentence-final punctuation at the end of a sentence's last word, opening quotes and brackets at the start of the first word.

When writing back, change only the words' text:

- Keep each word's id, timing and speaker as they are; the number and order of words do not change; write back every other field of the body exactly as read.
- **Allowed**: replace a word's text with the correct spelling (typos, homophone or near-homophone mishearings, spelling, capitalization, proper names); add, change or remove punctuation before or after a word's text; restore the spaces in a foreign-language phrase obviously run together inside one word (still within that word's text, not translated).
- **Not allowed**: merging or splitting words, adding or deleting words, reordering words, moving text onto other words, changing a word's text to an empty string.
- When one error spans several words and the correct spelling can be spread over those words with every word still having text, spread it (for example, in a character-by-character Chinese transcript, "深" "度" "雪" "洗" becomes "深" "度" "学" "习" (deep learning); in a word-by-word transcript, `Chat` `GBT` becomes `Chat` `GPT`). When it cannot be spread (it would only match by deleting a word or adding one), do not force it; list the spot and the correct spelling in the delivery notes.

Why so strict: every caption cue and every translated sentence is tied to these words' timings. You are changing the characters; the timeline must not move.

## 3. Before you start

Read the whole text first and settle these things; apply them throughout. They do not go into the deliverable:

- **Background reference**: first use `cuccut videos inspect` to look at the source asset's `assets[].source` (only assets imported from a link have it): title, uploader (`uploader`), description (`description`), the author's chapters. It is background reference, not transcript content, and not an absolute authority: the exact spellings of people, organizations, products and terms in it are strong correction hints, applied only when the speaker is clearly saying that thing; never add words or facts to the transcript just because the description has them. Spellings the user names are still hard requirements and take priority over it.
- **Content summary**: one or two sentences on what this video is about. What a misheard word really was mostly depends on it: in a video about machine learning, "深度雪洗" (deep snow wash, a mishearing of 深度学习, "deep learning") can only be "深度学习" (deep learning).
- **Terms and proper names**: recognize the different misspellings of the same term, person or product name, and unify them throughout to one correct spelling. Spellings the user names are hard requirements and are used verbatim: no inflection, no change in spelling or capitalization, no added or removed spaces. When the context cannot settle it, do not guess; leave it as is.
- **Source language**: take the transcript document's language. The polished text stays in that language and is never translated; words the speaker borrows from other languages stay as they are, and words of the source language are not swapped for another language.

## 4. Three things done by default

1. **Typos and mishearings**: obvious recognition errors, spelling, homophone or near-homophone mishearings, wrongly split word boundaries. Change them only with evidence from the context; awkward or non-standard phrasing in speech is not itself a recognition error - keep pronouns, tenses and spoken grammar as they are.
2. **Terms and proper names**: unify them as in section 3.
3. **Punctuation and sentence splits**: fix punctuation by meaning; whenever a complete idea has been said, close it with that writing system's own sentence-final punctuation.
   - Do not break a sentence after a dangling conjunction, preposition or an unfinished lead-in (for example `because.`, `of.`, `当。` (when, followed by a full stop), `和。` (and, followed by a full stop)): join it to the following clause and break once the idea is complete.
   - Pauses are only a hint: people often take a breath mid-sentence; split by meaning, not because of a pause.
   - Do not keep stringing a long stretch together with commas: a long stretch with no sentence-final punctuation gets hard-cut into very long sentences, and both captions and translations become hard to read.
   - Do not leave conflicting adjacent punctuation (for example `。，`, `，。`, `,,`, `.,`); keep only the one that marks the boundary.
   - Punctuation and spacing follow that writing system's own conventions: Chinese and Japanese use full-width punctuation with no spaces between characters; Latin, Cyrillic and other alphabetic scripts use half-width punctuation attached to the preceding word; other scripts follow their common writing norms - when unsure, keep the punctuation style already in the transcript, and do not borrow another script's punctuation.

A comparison of sentence splits (illustrative only):

Bad: `We tried three approaches back then, the first was going straight to a large model, the cost was too high, the second was distillation, quality dropped badly, in the end we used the third, the hybrid one,`

Good: `We tried three approaches back then. The first was going straight to a large model, the cost was too high. The second was distillation, quality dropped badly. In the end we used the third, the hybrid one.`

Not a single word moved; only the punctuation changed (plus the capital letters that follow it). But the first version gets cut into one caption that cannot fit, while in the second every sentence can stand as its own cue and be translated on its own.

## 5. Not done by default

- **Fixing grammar** (subject-verb agreement, articles, tenses and so on): only when the user asks, and only clear errors, without changing the meaning or tone; anything that would need words added or removed to fix is left alone and listed in the delivery notes.
- **Removing verbal tics, tightening rambling**: that means deleting words, which cannot be done in the transcript. If the user wants the video free of verbal tics and long pauses, that is editing: follow the talking-head cut (`talking-head-cut`) approach, or propose cuts with `cuccut edits apply`'s proposeCuts - cut the timeline, not the transcript.
- Rewriting, summarizing, reordering, adding content, translating: none of these.

When the user asks for one of these, first explain how it will affect captions and translations, then do the part that can be done.

## 6. Writing back

- Substitute the corrected text into the body you read and write it back to the same transcript with `cuccut documents put` (document is its documentId, kind unchanged), writing the whole transcript in one go.
- A version conflict means the user just edited it: read it again and redo the changes on the new body; never overwrite the user's edits with the old body.
- After writing, `cuccut documents read` once more and look at the sentences cut in translationBasis: no whole stretch run together into one sentence, and no break in the middle of a sentence; if not, fix the punctuation again.

## 7. Naming speakers

When the transcript distinguishes speakers, the body's `speakers[]` gives each speaker an id and a name. Automatic diarization gives only placeholder names; after polishing and writing back, the last thing to do is replace the placeholder names with real ones. Names appear in every caption cue and every exported file, so this step goes only by evidence, never by guessing.

- **Placeholder names**: the "Speaker n" the transcription flow assigns automatically and its equivalents in other UI languages (`说话人 1` (Speaker 1), `Sprecher 1`, `Parlante 1` - "speaker + number" names of that kind), numbered labels from the recognition service (`SPEAKER_00`, `S1`, `spk-1`), and names that are empty or equal to the id (case-insensitive). Any other name was given by the user or someone else; leave it alone.
- **When to do it**: required when there is more than one speaker and placeholder names remain; skip it when there is only one speaker or no placeholder names left. When polishing is skipped as section 1 describes, still do this step: it changes only the names, not the body. When the evidence can identify them, do not deliver a multi-speaker video with placeholder names.
- **Where evidence comes from**: about the first 400 words of the transcript; about 60 words before and 120 words after each speaker first speaks; the source asset's title, uploader and description (section 3); name captions (lower thirds) or on-screen text in frames: first use frames already grabbed in this task; when the metadata names participants but the transcript does not tie them to voices, use `cuccut videos frames` to grab a few frames from the first minute or two and where each speaker first speaks, and look for name captions. A name caption must clearly label the person who is speaking; a name that just happens to appear on screen does not count.
- **What counts as evidence**: a self-introduction ("I'm ...", "my name is ..."); an introduction by someone else ("today we have ...", "welcome, ..."); this speaker's response right after being addressed by name; a signature sign-off; source metadata that uniquely identifies one of them. When the metadata lists several guests but cannot tell which voice is whom, evidence from the transcript is still needed. A list of participants, the speaking order, speaker numbers and the topic itself are not evidence; conversely, when the title or description names participants, this step matters even more: find evidence for each one and match names to voices.
- **How to write the name**: the form actually used in the material, usually the full name, or whatever form appears when there is no full name (such as only a first name); keep the original script and spelling, no translation or transliteration; no titles, honorifics, organizations, brackets, quotes or explanations; at most 40 characters. When there is no name in the material but a role is stated clearly (host of a show, interviewer, narrator), a short role label may be used; never invent a role from the look of the conversation alone.
- **Do not guess**: when unsure, keep the placeholder name. A wrong guess is worse than leaving it: a wrong name appears in every caption cue and every exported file.
- **One person, several ids**: automatic diarization may split one person into several ids. When each id has its own evidence, give them the same name; do not merge ids.
- **Writing back**: write back to the same transcript with `cuccut documents put`, changing only `speakers[].name`, with words and other fields exactly as read; write all speakers in one go. On a version conflict, read again as in section 6.

## 8. What to avoid

- Do not turn speech into written prose, do not delete verbal tics, do not tighten, do not translate the foreign words mixed in.
- Do not merge, split, add, delete or reorder any word, and do not move text onto other words.
- Do not add a name or phrase to the transcript just because the description has it.
- Do not break sentences after dangling conjunctions or prepositions, and do not let a long stretch run on with commas.
- Do not guess speaker names; do not add titles or brackets to names.
- Do not overwrite a version the user just edited with the old body.

## 9. Delivery

- Explain: how many changes were made; which terms and proper names were unified; which sentence splits were added.
- List the spots not fixed because changes had to be word for word (the original and what it should be), and the spots left alone because you were unsure.
- Speakers: who was named and on what evidence (one sentence); who has no evidence and still has a placeholder name.
- When translating next, `cuccut documents read` the transcript again after this write-back.

## 10. Self-check

- The number of words, ids, timings and speakers match what was read; no word has empty text.
- Nothing was translated, rewritten, reordered or deleted; by default no grammar was fixed and no verbal tics were removed.
- Terms and proper names are consistent throughout, and spellings the user named appear verbatim.
- Every sentence closes with sentence-final punctuation, with no dangling breaks and no conflicting adjacent punctuation; punctuation and spacing fit that writing system's conventions.
- After writing back you read it again, and the sentences cut in translationBasis are a sensible length.
- With several speakers, no placeholder name remains that could have been identified; every name written has evidence, with no titles or brackets; names given by the user were not changed.
